Q: Best practice for modeling intermediary vs user-facing agents in LangGraph multi-agent workflows A:

This is a classic Architectural Scaling problem in LangGraph. When you outgrow a StateGraph, you have to shift from a shared-state mindset to a Modular Composition mindset.

Here is how to structure it using an Architectural approach:

1. The Monolithic Trap: Avoid "God State": The primary issue is a "God State"—one schema that every agent must understand. You should apply Interface Segregation. Intermediary agents usually need raw data (logs, tool outputs), while user-facing agents need refined context.

Use Sub-graphs. Create separate StateGraph instances for intermediary logic and the final user-facing response.

2. State Scoping: Use specialised Schemas: You don't need to share the entire state. LangGraph allows nodes to return a subset of the state or use Reducers.

  • Intermediary Agents: Use a PrivateState schema for internal reasoning.

  • User-facing Agents: Use a PublicState schema.

  • The Bridge: The Parent graph maps only the necessary outputs from the Intermediary sub-graph to the Public state. This eliminates coupling.

3. Solving the Streaming Bottleneck: If you put a user-facing agent deep inside a complex graph, streaming becomes a nightmare because the parent graph waits for node completion.

  • The Pattern: Use Command(goto=...) or Conditional Edges to hand off control to a "Terminal Node."

  • Streaming: Use astream_events with stream_mode="messages". This allows you to filter specifically for the user-facing agent's tokens while ignoring the "noise" of intermediary agent tool calls.

Should user-facing agents live outside?
No, keep them in a graph, but make them a Terminal Sub-graph. This keeps the logic versioned and testable.

Split workflows or separate graphs?
Use Parent-Child graphs. The parent handles high-level routing; children handle specialized tasks.

Recommended pattern?
The "Router-Worker" pattern. A Router (Intermediate) decides the path, and a Worker (User-facing) generates the final response.

Q: How to properly use colorScheme in Flutter? A:

That's a great question and actually it also bothers me.

What I understand is the following:

In Color scheme, you define the primary, secondary and tertiary colors. You can define some more like, surface, on surface, etc.

Let's say you define as primary color the color Colors.red.

According to the Material 3 Design, primary color affects the color of buttons ( among other widgets). That means that from now on, your buttons will be colored based on the primary color red. (I.e. Filled Button)

Now, it's cool having all filled buttons red in your app and instead of having to define everytime the color of the button whenever you want to use one, right?

But let's say, you have a screen somewhere, where you want to use a filled button that is colored with the color blue. A common practice is to create your own UI library with the widgets your app is using. For instance for the blue button you create a MyCustomBlueButton widget that is a wrapper to the filled button and the only thing it does is it overrides the color of the filled button and uses the color blue instead. That's a case where you want to use Colors instead of primary. Imho, it's a good practice to avoid using Colors directly in your project. Define in a UI folder all the widgets your app is using, and then use them in your app. That way ylifnyou want to change a color of let's say a button, you don't have to go throught all your files in your main project, you just change the color of the button in the UI folder.

Additional notes:

Do you have define a color scheme at all? Not at all. You can hard code define all colors of your app in a file in the UI folder and use them in your widgets.

Would I define color scheme? yes, defining color scheme helps a lot because it auto define the colors for the dark theme. So having a defined color scheme will automatically generate the colors for the dark theme.

Also, it makes it easier to kick start your app and it saves you time.

Q: How can I split a single file from a git repo into a new repo? A:

Use git fast-export.

First you export the history of the file to a fast-import stream (.fi file). Make sure you do this on the master branch.

cd oldrepo
git fast-export HEAD -- MyFile.ext >../myfile.fi

Then you create a new repo and import.

cd ..
mkdir newrepo
cd newrepo
git init
git fast-import <../myfile.fi
git checkout

Q: Custom ratio contrasts with emmeans and glmmTMB A:

What you’re running into here isn’t really a glmmTMB or emmeans limitation, it’s a math issue.

emmeans::contrast() only works with linear contrasts (additions and subtractions of means). A ratio like

exposure ÷ average(baseline)

is not linear, so dividing contrast vectors (e.g. level2 / baseline) can’t work and will never give a valid result.

The standard way this is handled (and the way it’s done in industry) is to work on the log scale.

The key idea is:

A ratio of means is just the exponentiated difference of log-means.

So instead of trying to compute the ratio directly, you:

  1. Get the marginal means with emmeans

  2. Re-express them on the log scale

  3. Define your custom contrasts as simple differences (e.g. exposure − average baseline)

  4. Back-transform the results

emmeans handles all of this correctly, including standard errors, confidence intervals, and multiplicity adjustments.

The final output is exactly what you want:

  • Estimates are ratios

  • Confidence intervals are asymmetric and valid

  • p-values are correct

  • Interpretation matches how ratios are typically reported
